bless.gloss: To ask God's favor on someone or something, to make something holy, or — in the passive — to be lucky enough to have something good.

senses.head: Ask God's favor on
senses.body: The core religious sense: a priest, a parent, or a speaker calls down protection or good fortune on a person. Neutral in American English and common well outside church.
examples: The priest *blessed* the fleet on the first Sunday in June.
Her mother *blesses* the children before every long trip.
The bishop *had blessed* the building long before the first class met in it.

senses.head: Consecrate, make holy
senses.body: Used of objects, water, buildings, and ground rather than of people; the thing becomes sacred or set apart.
examples: A rabbi came to *bless* the new sanctuary.
They *blessed* the ground before a single shovel went in.
That chapel *has been blessed* by three different bishops.

senses.head: Be blessed with
senses.body: Passive only, and usually entirely secular: to be lucky enough to have some good quality, person, or circumstance.
examples: We *have been blessed* with patient neighbors.
He *was blessed* with a good ear and no patience at all.

senses.head: Bless you; bless your heart
senses.body: Fixed conversational phrases: *bless you* after a sneeze or as warm thanks, and Southern *bless your heart*, which is sincere sympathy or a soft insult depending entirely on tone.
examples: *Bless* you — that is exactly what I needed today.
*Bless* her heart, she tried to fix the sink herself and made it worse.

burn.gloss: To be on fire or destroy by fire, and by extension to scorch, sting, consume fuel, or be consumed by a strong feeling.

senses.head: Be on fire; destroy by fire
senses.body: Works in both directions: the thing burns, or someone burns it. The literal sense that every other one grows out of.
examples: Dry pine *burns* fast and throws sparks.
Vandals *burned* the shed to the ground.
The barn *has burned* twice since the family bought the place.

senses.head: Scorch food, overcook
senses.body: Of food left too long on heat, and of the cook who left it there. Nothing is on fire — the food is just ruined.
examples: I *burned* the first batch of cookies and started over.
Don't let the sauce *burn* while you set the table.
She *has burned* every pot in this kitchen at least once.

senses.head: Injure with heat or chemicals
senses.body: Of skin damaged by heat, steam, acid, or friction. Often reflexive or with a body part as object — *burn yourself*, *burn your hand*.
examples: He *burned* his hand on the oven rack.
Steam *had burned* her wrist before she got the lid off.

senses.head: Redden in the sun
senses.body: Intransitive, of skin or of a person in strong sun. *Tan* is what happens when you don't burn.
examples: I *burn* in about fifteen minutes without sunscreen.
His shoulders *burned* on the very first day of the trip.

senses.head: Use as fuel; use up
senses.body: Of fuel, calories, money, and time — the resource is consumed. *Burn through* stresses how fast it goes.
examples: The old furnace *burns* about a gallon an hour.
We *burned* half the budget on the first prototype.
She *has burned* through three phone chargers this year.

senses.head: Sting, feel hot
senses.body: Of a body part or a strong taste producing a hot, painful sensation. No injury is implied.
examples: The smoke *burned* my eyes all the way down the trail.
My throat *has burned* since the fire started.
That pepper will *burn* for a good ten minutes.

senses.head: Be consumed by a feeling
senses.body: *Burn with* shame, anger, or curiosity; also *be burning to* do something, meaning impatient. Literary but still current.
examples: Her face *burned* when they read the letter out loud.
Kids *burn* with curiosity at that age.
He *has burned* with resentment about that promotion for two years.

senses.head: Burn out
senses.body: Of a bulb, motor, or fuse: stop working for good. Of a person: collapse from sustained overwork — the source of the noun *burnout*.
examples: Nurses *burn* out fastest in their third year.
The porch light *burned* out again.
Two of the residents *have burned* out and left medicine entirely.

senses.head: Get burned (be cheated)
senses.body: Informal and figurative, almost always passive: to be cheated, betrayed, or badly hurt by trusting someone or something.
examples: Investors *got burned* when the company folded.
I *have been burned* by contractors twice, so I ask for references now.

senses.head: Copy data to a disc
senses.body: To write files to a CD or DVD. Peak-2005 vocabulary and fading with the hardware, but still instantly understood.
examples: He *burned* the whole album onto a CD for the drive.
I *have burned* a backup disc for every project since that crash.

chap.gloss: Of skin, to crack and turn sore in cold or dry air; in older use, to split or crack open generally.

senses.head: Of skin, crack and redden
senses.body: Both ways: skin chaps, or wind and cold chap it. In modern American English the verb lives mostly in its participle used as an adjective — *chapped lips*, *chapped hands*.
examples: Wind like this *chaps* your face in ten minutes.
My hands *chapped* badly the first winter we lived in Minnesota.
His lips *have chapped* every January since he was a kid.
By March her knuckles *had chapped* and split open.

senses.head: Split, crack open
senses.body: The wider old sense, of dry ground, wood, or paint rather than skin. Archaic outside dialect; you will meet it only in older writing.
examples: Drought will *chap* bare ground faster than anyone expects.
The clay *chapped* into plates all across the riverbed.

clap.gloss: To strike your palms together in applause, and by extension to slap someone in friendly greeting or to put something somewhere abruptly.

senses.head: Applaud
senses.body: The everyday sense. Intransitive, or with *for* — *they clapped for her*; you clap a performance, not a person, when the verb is transitive.
examples: The whole room *claps* at the end of every set.
She *clapped* until her hands stung.
The audience *has clapped* through six straight curtain calls.

senses.head: Clap someone on the back
senses.body: Almost always *clap someone on the back* or *on the shoulder* — a hearty gesture of congratulation, never aggression.
examples: He *clapped* me on the shoulder and walked off without a word.
Coaches *clap* their players on the back after a bad inning too.

senses.head: Put abruptly or forcefully
senses.body: Sudden, forceful placement: *clap a hand over someone's mouth*, *clap on the brakes*, or the old *clap him in irons*. The speed is the point.
examples: She *clapped* a hand over her mouth before the laugh got out.
They *had clapped* him in jail before his lawyer even heard about it.

senses.head: Clap eyes on
senses.body: Informal fixed phrase about a first or only sighting, and common in the negative: *I've never clapped eyes on him*.
examples: The minute she *clapped* eyes on the house she wanted it.
I *had* never *clapped* eyes on the man before that morning.

dip.gloss: To put something briefly into a liquid, and by extension to drop, to slope downward, or to reach into a supply.

senses.head: Put briefly into liquid
senses.body: In and straight back out again — that brevity is what separates *dip* from *soak* or *submerge*.
examples: He *dips* his bread in the olive oil before every bite.
She *dipped* a toe in the lake and decided against swimming.
I *have dipped* the whole tray of strawberries in chocolate already.

senses.head: Drop, decline briefly
senses.body: Of numbers, prices, or temperature: down and usually back up. A permanent fall *drops* or *falls*; a *dip* is expected to recover.
examples: The temperature *dipped* below freezing overnight.
Sales *have dipped* for three quarters in a row.
Ratings always *dip* in the second week of a run.

senses.head: Slope downward
senses.body: Of a road, a piece of land, or a rock layer that angles down; also of a bird or plane losing height for a moment.
examples: The road *dips* twice before the bridge.
The trail *had dipped* into fog before we ever saw the sign.

senses.head: Dip into
senses.body: Two uses of the same picture, both meaning to take a little: money out of savings, or a few pages out of a book you never read straight through.
examples: We *dipped* into savings to cover the roof.
I *have dipped* into that biography three times and never finished it.
Feel free to *dip* into the report wherever it interests you.

senses.head: Lower briefly
senses.body: Of a flag, a head, a wing, or headlights. Note that headlights turned down are *dipped beams* in British English but *low beams* in American.
examples: Ships *dip* their flags when they pass a naval vessel.
He *dipped* his head and went back to work.

senses.head: Scoop out
senses.body: To lift liquid out with a container. Old-fashioned and regional in American English, where *scoop* or *ladle* is the ordinary word.
examples: She *dipped* water from the barrel with a tin cup.
The boys *had dipped* the trough dry by noon.

dwell.gloss: To keep thinking or talking about something, or — in older and literary use — to live somewhere.

senses.head: Dwell on, dwell upon
senses.body: Everyday American English and by far the most common use of the verb. Usually about something painful you would be better off letting go.
examples: Don't *dwell* on one bad review.
She *dwelt* on the subject for most of the drive home.
He *dwells* on every mistake he has ever made.
The speech *had dwelt* so long on the budget that it lost the room.

senses.head: Live, reside
senses.body: The original sense, now literary or biblical in American English — *live* is the ordinary word. Perfectly clear, just elevated.
examples: They *dwell* in a cabin two miles from the nearest paved road.
Her people *dwelt* in that valley for four generations.
He *has dwelt* in the same apartment since 1994.

senses.head: Be lodged in, persist within
senses.body: Figurative extension of the *live* sense: a feeling or quality stays inside a person or a place. Literary in register.
examples: A quiet resentment *dwelt* in him for years.
Something like hope *has dwelt* in that congregation through worse than this.

enwrap.gloss: To wrap something completely around or inside something else, or figuratively to absorb someone's whole attention — literary in both senses.

senses.head: Wrap completely, envelop
senses.body: Literary; in ordinary American prose *wrap*, *envelop*, or *swaddle* is the natural choice. Often of fog, cloth, or darkness covering something entirely.
examples: Museums *enwrap* fragile pieces in acid-free tissue before they ship them.
She *enwrapped* the child in a quilt and carried her inside.
Silence *has enwrapped* the valley since the mill closed.

senses.head: Absorb entirely, engross
senses.body: Usually passive — *enwrapped in thought*. Rare and old-fashioned, and constantly confused with *rapt* 'entranced', which is a separate word; *enwrapt* is only an archaic spelling of this verb.
examples: He *was enwrapped* in the argument and never heard the bell.
The book *had enwrapped* her so completely that she missed her stop.

indwell.gloss: To live or be present within something, especially in a spiritual sense — a narrow word met mostly as the adjective *indwelling*.

senses.head: Be present within (spiritually)
senses.body: Theological vocabulary: the Spirit, grace, or God indwells a believer. The finite forms are genuinely rare, and the past and participle are *indwelt*, never *indwelled*.
examples: Theologians argue about how grace can *indwell* a person at all.
The doctrine holds that grace *indwells* the believer.
Older translations say the Spirit *indwelt* the apostles.
That conviction *has indwelt* the community for three centuries.

senses.head: Pervade, be lodged in
senses.body: Extended literary use for a quality or mood that seems to live inside a person, a text, or a building.
examples: A quiet stubbornness *indwelt* every sentence she wrote.
Something like grief *had indwelt* the house long before we bought it.

learn.gloss: To take in knowledge or a skill, or to find something out.

senses.head: Acquire knowledge or a skill
senses.body: The central sense, with a subject or skill as object. Note that *learn* is what the student does; the teacher *teaches*.
examples: Kids *learn* the alphabet before they learn to read.
He *learned* Spanish in eight months of night classes.
We *have learned* a lot from the first two rounds of testing.

senses.head: Find out, hear of
senses.body: Followed by *that*, *of*, or *about*. Slightly more formal than *find out*, and the standard verb in news writing.
examples: I *learned* about the closure from a neighbor.
We *learn* of most changes the same week the customers do.
By Friday they *had learned* that the grant would not be renewed.

senses.head: Learn to do something
senses.body: With an infinitive: gain an ability, or come to accept a way of living. *She learned to say no* is about habit as much as skill.
examples: He *learned* to drive on a farm truck.
You *learn* to live with the noise.
I *have learned* to keep my mouth shut in those meetings.

senses.head: Memorize
senses.body: With a text, part, or piece as object, often with *by heart*. The result is recall, not understanding.
examples: She *learned* the whole part in four days.
The choir *has learned* three new pieces this season.
Actors *learn* their lines before the first rehearsal.

senses.head: Learn from; learn your lesson
senses.body: To be changed by an experience, usually an unpleasant one. The fixed phrase is *learn your lesson*, often sarcastic in the negative.
examples: He never *learned* his lesson about lending money to family.
We *have learned* from every outage this year.

senses.head: Teach (nonstandard)
senses.body: Dialectal and jokey only — *that'll learn you*, *I'll learn him*. Never write it in standard prose; the standard verb is *teach*.
examples: That'll *learn* you to leave the gate open.
His uncle *learned* him to shoot before he was ten.

misspell.gloss: To write a word with the wrong letters.

senses.head: Write a word with wrong letters
senses.body: Transitive, with the word or name as object, and very often used about names on signs, plaques, and official documents. American *misspelled*, British *misspelt*.
examples: Autocorrect *misspells* her last name every single time.
He *misspelled* "necessary" twice in the same paragraph.
Reporters routinely *misspell* the town's name.
The engraver *has misspelled* the donor's name on the plaque.
Nobody noticed that the sign *had misspelled* "restaurant" until it was hung.
I *misspelled* it on the form and had to start the whole thing over.

nip.gloss: To give a small sharp bite or pinch — and, of cold, to sting.

senses.head: Bite or pinch sharply
senses.body: A quick, small bite that does not tear — of dogs, crabs, and horses, usually with *at* when it is a habit rather than one event.
examples: The puppy *nips* at your ankles whenever he gets excited.
A crab *nipped* his finger in the tide pool.
The dog *has nipped* two people at the park this month.

senses.head: Of cold, sting
senses.body: Of frost or wind against skin or plants. The adjective *nippy*, meaning chilly, comes straight from this sense.
examples: A wind off the lake will *nip* your fingers right through gloves.
Frost *nipped* the tomatoes on the first cold night.
The wind *had nipped* their faces raw by the second mile.

senses.head: Nip in the bud
senses.body: Fixed phrase: stop something small before it can grow. The common mishearing *nip it in the butt* is an error, not a variant.
examples: We *nipped* that rumor in the bud before it reached the board.
Good managers *nip* this kind of thing in the bud.

senses.head: Pinch off, snip
senses.body: Gardening use: remove a bud, tip, or shoot with fingers or small shears so the plant grows fuller.
examples: *Nip* the side shoots off as they appear.
She *had nipped* every dead bloom off the bush by Sunday.

senses.head: Take a small drink
senses.body: Usually *nip at* something alcoholic. The noun — *a nip*, a small measure of liquor — is far more common than the verb.
examples: He *nipped* at a flask all through the ceremony.
They *have nipped* at that bottle since noon.

senses.head: Go quickly (British)
senses.body: British only — *nip out for milk*, *nip round to a friend's*. An American says *run out* or *pop over*, and reads this use as distinctly foreign.
examples: I'll just *nip* out for milk.
She *nipped* round to her mother's before work.

relearn.gloss: To learn again something you once knew and lost.

senses.head: Learn again after forgetting
senses.body: The core sense: injury, disuse, or plain forgetting has taken a skill away and you build it back. For changing careers American English says *retrain*, not *relearn*.
examples: Stroke patients often *relearn* to walk before they relearn to speak.
After the surgery he *relearned* the fingering one hand at a time.
She *has relearned* enough French to get through a menu.
By August the team *had relearned* the whole playbook.

senses.head: Come to understand again
senses.body: Of lessons and truths rather than skills: something you already knew gets driven home a second time, usually with a note of irony.
examples: Every generation *relearns* that shortcuts cost more later.
We *relearned* the value of backups the expensive way.
He *relearned* the route the hard way, one wrong turn at a time.

smell.gloss: To perceive an odor, or to give one off — and figuratively, to sense that something is wrong.

senses.head: Perceive an odor
senses.body: The passive perception, usually with *can*: *I can smell rain*. A state verb here, so the progressive is odd — not *I am smelling smoke*.
examples: I can *smell* rain coming before I see the clouds.
He *smelled* gas the second he opened the door.
The dogs *have smelled* something under the porch.

senses.head: Sniff at deliberately
senses.body: The active version — you put your nose to something on purpose. Unlike sense 1, this one takes the progressive: *she's smelling the milk*.
examples: She *smells* the milk before she pours it.
He *smelled* the cork and nodded.

senses.head: Give off an odor
senses.body: With *like*, *of*, or an adjective — *smells wonderful*, *smells like smoke*. Here the subject is the source of the smell, not the person noticing it.
examples: The whole apartment *smelled* like burnt popcorn.
Fresh basil *smells* nothing like the dried kind.
The room *had smelled* faintly of paint for weeks.

senses.head: Stink
senses.body: With no complement at all, *smell* means smell bad: *this room smells*. Add an adjective and the negative meaning disappears.
examples: That cooler *smells*; take it out to the garage.
The gym bag *has smelled* like that since June.

senses.head: Sense that something is wrong
senses.body: Figurative and informal but extremely common: *smell trouble*, *smell a rat*, *smell blood*.
examples: I *smell* a rat in the way that contract was awarded.
The reporters *smelled* a story and started calling everyone.
Investigators *had smelled* trouble long before the audit began.

senses.head: Reek of, suggest (figurative)
senses.body: *Smell of* or *smell like* with an abstract noun: the situation gives an impression, and almost always a bad one.
examples: The whole plan *smells* of desperation.
That settlement *has smelled* like a cover-up from day one.

spell.gloss: To give the letters of a word in order — and, figuratively, to mean or signal something.

senses.head: Say or write a word's letters
senses.body: The central sense, and the one behind *spelling bee* and *can't spell*.
examples: He *spells* his last name for people over the phone every day.
She *spelled* the street name wrong on the envelope.
I *have spelled* it both ways and neither one looks right.
*Spell* it slowly for me and I will write it down.

senses.head: Of letters, form a word
senses.body: Here the subject is the letters themselves: *C-A-T spells cat*. Also used of acronyms that accidentally form a word.
examples: Those four letters *spell* her grandmother's name.
The initials *spelled* something unfortunate, so they changed the title.

senses.head: Mean, signal (spell trouble)
senses.body: Almost always with a bad outcome as object: *spells trouble*, *spells disaster*, *spells the end of*. The subject is a situation, never a person.
examples: Another dry summer *spells* trouble for the whole valley.
The 2008 crash *spelled* the end for a lot of small firms.
That memo *has spelled* doom for the project since the day it went out.

senses.head: Spell out (explain plainly)
senses.body: To state something in terms nobody can miss, often with an edge of impatience — *do I have to spell it out?*
examples: Let me *spell* it out for you.
She *spelled* out exactly what would happen if we missed the date.
The contract *had spelled* out the penalty in the first paragraph.

senses.head: Spell out (write in full)
senses.body: The editorial sense: give the whole word or number in letters instead of a symbol or an abbreviation.
examples: Style guides ask you to *spell* out numbers under ten.
He *spelled* out the state name instead of using the postal code.

senses.head: Relieve, take over for
senses.body: Chiefly American: to give someone a break by taking their work for a while. Related to the noun *a spell*, meaning a stretch of time.
examples: I'll *spell* you at the wheel after the next exit.
Two neighbors *spelled* her at the hospital so she could sleep.
Volunteers *have spelled* the crew every four hours.

spill.gloss: To let liquid or loose material fall out of its container — and figuratively, to let information out.

senses.head: Let liquid fall out
senses.body: Transitive and normally accidental; deliberate emptying is *pour out* or *dump*.
examples: I *spilled* coffee on the keyboard an hour before the demo.
Kids *spill* things; that is what the mat is for.
Someone *has spilled* juice on the back seat.

senses.head: Of contents, run out
senses.body: Intransitive, with the liquid or the loose material itself as subject — grain, gravel, and beads spill as readily as water.
examples: Don't fill it that high or it *spills* every time you move it.
The truck *had spilled* gravel across both lanes.

senses.head: Pour out of a place
senses.body: Of a crowd, or of light and sound, leaving a space in quantity: *spilled into the street*, *light spilling from a doorway*.
examples: Fans *spilled* into the street after the final out.
Light *has spilled* from that window every night since he moved in.

senses.head: Reveal a secret
senses.body: Informal: *spill the beans*, *spill the details*, or simply *spill it*. The newer slang *spill the tea* is the same idea.
examples: She *spilled* the whole story before dessert arrived.
Come on, *spill* it.
Someone in the office *has spilled* the details to a reporter.

senses.head: Spill over
senses.body: Of a conflict, a cost, or a crowd that will not stay inside its boundary.
examples: The dispute *spilled* over into the neighboring county.
Overtime costs *have spilled* over into next year's budget.

senses.head: Throw from a seat; take a fall
senses.body: Dated as a verb — *the horse spilled him at the fence* — though the noun stays alive in *took a nasty spill*.
examples: The horse *spilled* him at the second fence.
Two riders *had spilled* on the same corner before the race was stopped.

spoil.gloss: To ruin something good, to let food go bad, or to treat someone too generously.

senses.head: Ruin, mar
senses.body: Something that was fine is made worse, usually by one intruding factor. In elections, a *spoiled ballot* is one marked so it cannot be counted.
examples: Rain *spoiled* the second half of the game.
One loud table can *spoil* a whole evening.
The argument *has spoiled* every holiday since.

senses.head: Of food, go bad
senses.body: Intransitive, of milk, meat, and produce; the transitive version puts the heat or the delay in the subject slot.
examples: Cream *spoils* fast in a warm car.
The heat *had spoiled* everything in the cooler by noon.

senses.head: Indulge, pamper (a child)
senses.body: Critical: too much giving has made the person selfish. Hence *a spoiled child*; British English writes *spoilt* here especially often.
examples: Her grandparents *have spoiled* those kids since the day they were born.
He *spoiled* the dog until it refused to eat anything from a can.

senses.head: Treat generously (positive)
senses.body: The friendly version of sense 3, about a treat rather than a character flaw: *spoil yourself*, *they spoiled us all weekend*.
examples: *Spoil* yourself — you have earned it.
Her hosts *spoiled* her rotten for four days.

senses.head: Give away the ending
senses.body: Modern and very common, and the source of the noun *spoiler*: to reveal a plot point to someone who has not seen it yet.
examples: Don't *spoil* the twist for anyone who hasn't seen it.
He *spoiled* the surprise about ten minutes early.
Someone in the group chat *has spoiled* the finale for everybody.

senses.head: Be spoiling for
senses.body: Fixed and -ing only: eager for a confrontation. You cannot unwind it into other tenses — not *he spoiled for a fight*.
examples: He *is spoiling* for a fight and has been all week.
The whole room *was spoiling* for an argument.

sunburn.gloss: To get, or to give someone, red sore skin from too much sun.

senses.head: Burn one's skin in the sun
senses.body: Works both ways: a person or a patch of skin sunburns, or the sun sunburns them. In practice Americans prefer *get sunburned* or *get a sunburn* to the plain finite verb.
examples: Pale skin *sunburns* in twenty minutes on that beach.
He *sunburned* the back of his neck on the very first day.
We *sunburn* easily, so we go out early or late.
I *have sunburned* my shoulders every summer of my life.
By the third afternoon everyone *had sunburned* except the lifeguard.

senses.head: Weather, redden permanently
senses.body: Almost always the participle used as an adjective, describing skin darkened and roughened by years outdoors rather than one bad afternoon. *Sunburned* is American, *sunburnt* more British.
examples: Years of roofing *had sunburned* his forearms to leather.
The farmer's face *was sunburned* and lined from forty seasons outdoors.

toss.gloss: To throw something lightly, and by extension to discard it, mix it, or move it around restlessly.

senses.head: Throw lightly
senses.body: A short, casual, underhand throw — nothing like the force of *hurl* or the aim of *pitch*.
examples: He *tosses* the keys on the counter the second he walks in.
She *tossed* the ball back over the fence.
Someone *has tossed* a jacket over the railing.

senses.head: Throw away, get rid of
senses.body: *Toss* or *toss out*, both everyday American speech where British English says *chuck*.
examples: Just *toss* the receipt; we don't need it.
He *tossed* the leftovers without asking anyone.
I *have tossed* out three boxes of old paperwork this week.

senses.head: Mix lightly
senses.body: Cooking: lift and turn ingredients so a dressing or coating reaches everything without crushing it.
examples: *Toss* the salad right before you serve it.
She *tossed* the pasta with oil and lemon.

senses.head: Flip a coin to decide
senses.body: *Toss a coin*, *toss for it*, and in sports *win the toss*. The noun *a toss-up* — an even chance — comes from here.
examples: They *tossed* a coin for the last seat on the flight.
We *have tossed* for the top bunk every summer since we were six.

senses.head: Move restlessly; be thrown about
senses.body: Of a sleeper — the fixed pair is *toss and turn* — and of a boat in rough water.
examples: He *tossed* and turned until the alarm went off.
The boat *had tossed* all night, and nobody slept.

senses.head: Jerk the head or hair
senses.body: A quick upward movement of the head, and always a gesture — pride, impatience, or dismissal.
examples: She *tossed* her hair and walked out.
The horse *has tossed* its head at every car that passes.

senses.head: Dismiss, throw out (a case)
senses.body: American news and sports usage: a judge tosses a lawsuit, an umpire tosses a player out of the game.
examples: The judge *tossed* the case for lack of evidence.
An appeals court *has tossed* two of the three charges.

senses.head: Toss around (an idea)
senses.body: To discuss possibilities loosely, without committing to any of them.
examples: We *tossed* around a few names for the shop.
They *have tossed* that idea around for years and never acted on it.

unlearn.gloss: To deliberately get rid of a habit, an assumption, or a piece of knowledge you already have.

senses.head: Get rid of a habit or skill
senses.body: Of trained behavior — form, technique, an accent — that has to come out before anything better goes in. The effort is deliberate; simply forgetting is not unlearning.
examples: New coaches spend the first month getting players to *unlearn* bad form.
She *unlearned* the accent she grew up with and later wished she hadn't.
By then the team *had unlearned* the shortcuts that caused the outage.

senses.head: Discard a belief or assumption
senses.body: Of ideas rather than skills: what you were taught and now reject. Common in modern writing about bias, education, and management.
examples: I *have unlearned* almost everything that class taught me about commas.
Some things are harder to *unlearn* than to learn in the first place.
A whole generation *has unlearned* the idea that the office is the only place work happens.

vex.gloss: To annoy or trouble someone, especially over a stretch of time.

senses.head: Annoy, irritate
senses.body: Formal and slightly old-fashioned in American speech, where *annoy* or *bug* is the everyday word; *vexing* and *vexed* stay current in writing.
examples: Slow permits *vexed* the developer for two full years.
It does not take much to *vex* him before his first cup of coffee.
Small delays *vex* her far more than big ones do.

senses.head: Baffle, resist solution
senses.body: Of a question or problem that will not yield — the sense behind *a vexed question* and *a vexing issue*. The problem is the subject and the people working on it are the object.
examples: The same question *vexes* every committee that looks at it.
That inconsistency *has vexed* editors since the style guide came out.
The problem *had vexed* mathematicians for a century before anyone cracked it.

senses.head: Afflict, harass (archaic)
senses.body: The old strong sense — storms, illness, or enemies tormenting a person or a country. You meet it in the King James Bible and older literature, not in modern American prose.
examples: Storms *vexed* the coast all that winter.
A fever *had vexed* the camp for a month.

wrap.gloss: To cover something by folding material around it — and figuratively, to finish, to enfold, or to be absorbed in something.

senses.head: Cover by folding material around
senses.body: Paper, foil, or cloth folded over an object until it is covered. The everyday sense.
examples: She *wraps* every gift in plain brown paper.
He *wrapped* the leftovers and put them in the fridge.
I *have wrapped* half the presents and hidden none of them.

senses.head: Wind around
senses.body: The material goes around the thing rather than over it — a scarf, a bandage, a cord, an arm.
examples: *Wrap* the pipes before the first hard freeze.
She *wrapped* a towel around her hair.
Vines *have wrapped* themselves around the whole trellis.

senses.head: Wrap up (finish)
senses.body: To bring a meeting, a job, or a deal to a close. *Let's wrap up* is standard American office speech.
examples: Let's *wrap* this up before lunch.
We *wrapped* up the audit two days early.
The committee *has wrapped* up its work for the year.

senses.head: Finish filming
senses.body: Film and television: production ends. Hence the announcement *that's a wrap* and the noun *wrap party*.
examples: They *wrap* on Friday no matter where the schedule stands.
The crew *had wrapped* the shoot two days early.

senses.head: Wrap up (dress warmly)
senses.body: Intransitive or reflexive: *wrap up warm*, *wrapped up in a parka*. Heard more in British speech but understood everywhere.
examples: *Wrap* up — it's ten degrees out there.
The kids *were wrapped* up to the eyes and still cold.

senses.head: Be wrapped up in
senses.body: Passive only: so absorbed in something that nothing else registers. Also *wrapped up in each other*.
examples: He *was wrapped* up in the game and never heard the phone.
She *has been wrapped* up in that manuscript for months.

senses.head: Wrap your head around
senses.body: Informal fixed phrase for finally understanding something difficult, and usually negative — *I can't wrap my head around it*.
examples: I still can't *wrap* my head around the numbers.
Nobody *has wrapped* their head around what the new rule actually requires.

senses.head: Wrap a car around something
senses.body: Colloquial American, and only in this frame: *wrap a car around* a pole or a tree, describing a violent head-on crash.
examples: He *wrapped* his truck around a utility pole on the county road.
Two kids *had wrapped* a car around that same tree the year before.
